diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Proposed change: add a 32-word unrolled loop ahead of the 16-word loop

**Reasoning.** Every variant so far (Attempts 1–3 and the top programs) has the same cost, 3836, even though the tail structure changed. That suggests the cost is dominated by the per-word popcount work, which no restructuring of the tail can reduce. The part of the loop that can still shrink is the per-iteration overhead: each trip through `for len(xs) >= 16` pays for a length compare, a branch, and a reslice (`xs = xs[16:]`). Doubling the block size to 32 halves the number of those trips for large inputs. The 16-word loop and the existing tail stay in place to handle the remainder, so the result is unchanged for every input length.

I have not measured this. If giri counts the reslice and loop-header instructions as I expect, the gain is modest; if the popcount calls dominate, the cost stays at 3836. The change is correct either way, since the 32-word loop only runs while at least 32 words remain and the 16-word loop and tail handle what is left.
